newsitem.title: USA: Mars has long intrigued scientists, movie makers.
newsitem.headline: Mars has long intrigued scientists, movie makers.

text.p: With its red surface and close proximity to Earth, the planet Mars has long been a source of fascination for scientists, space buffs and Hollywood screenwriters.
Named after the Roman god of war and the state, Mars is about half the size of Earth and twice the size of the moon. A day on Mars is slightly longer than one on Earth -- 24 hours and 37 minutes.

Of all the planets in the solar system, Mars is the most like Earth, and if Friday's Pathfinder mission proves successful, scientists say Mars is the most likely candidate for manned exploration early next century.
"Mars is an incredible planet," Dan Goldin, administrator of the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, told reporters on Thursday. "It has an unbelievable pull on the imagination."
Indeed, from the 1600s, when observers tried to calculate the length of a day on Mars, to the Pathfinder's high-tech exploration, Mars has attracted considerable attention.

Author H.G. Wells, sensing the world's fascination with the Red Planet, provided an early look at what Martians might be like in his 1898 novel "War of the Worlds," which depicted a Martian invasion of Earth.

Forty years later, Orson Welles triggered widespread panic with a radio dramatisation of the novel. After that, Hollywood repeatedly turned to Mars for ideas, often depicting "little green men" bent on destroying the Earth.
But it was not until last year that scientists actually had some evidence that suggested primitive life may once have existed on Mars.

Using data from a 4.5 billion-year-old meteorite found in Antarctica, scientists announced last August that the rock contained fossil evidence of what they believe may have been ancient micro-organisms, suggesting that Mars may have supported life more than 3.6 billion years ago.
The revelation, which followed a two-year investigation by scientists from NASA, reignited debate on an age-old question: Are we alone in the universe?

In Roswell, New Mexico, where thousands of space buffs and alien enthusiasts are gathering this weekend to celebrate the 50th anniversary of an alleged landing by creatures from outer space, the answer is no.

Most said they firmly believed that a spacecraft slammed into the New Mexico desert on the night of July 4, 1947, and that its alien crew, killed in the crash, was taken away for top-secret tests by the U.S. Air Force.

The Air Force last week released a report saying the alleged wreckage of the UFO was, in fact, that of a top-secret military balloon used to monitor Soviet nuclear tests at the start of the Cold War. The aliens reported by Roswell witnesses, the report said, were most likely dummies used to test high-altitude parachutes a decade later.
But many people dismiss the government's explanation and believe there is some form of life in outer space.

In 2005, NASA plans to send to Mars a robotic spacecraft that will be able to return soil and rock samples to Earth for more intensive study. If these tests prove successful, NASA may decide to send a manned exploration to Mars, similar to the Apollo landings on the Moon almost 30 years ago.

According to current theories, Mars may once have been much warmer and humid. Surfaces of Mars show what appear to be ancient lakes, suggesting that water flowed on the surface at one time and some form of life may have survived.
Scientists hope the exploration of Mars will help them learn what caused the planet's fate to change and perhaps provide some clues to prevent a similar change on Earth.
